strengths: OmniX provides a practical, unified formulation that repurposes pre-trained 2D flow matching models (FLUX.1-dev) for a broad spectrum of panoramic tasks, including generation, intrinsic decomposition (albedo, roughness, metallic), geometry estimation (distance, surface normals), and masked completion.
The exploration and ablation of DiT adapter architectures (Shared-Branch vs. Shared-Adapter vs. Separate-Adapter) is well-executed and provides clear empirical justification for the chosen design.
The creation of the PanoX dataset fills a noticeable gap in panoramic vision by offering high-quality indoor and outdoor equirectangular images paired with dense PBR material maps and geometry.

Demonstrating end-to-end integration into a graphics engine (Blender) with physically based rendering, interactive exploration, and dynamic physics simulations effectively showcases the downstream utility of the predicted intrinsic maps.
weaknesses: Although presented as a unified framework, the system requires training 12 separate adapter models for different modalities and fill tasks, rather than operating as a single unified multi-task or multi-modal backbone.
The PanoX dataset is derived from only 8 distinct synthetic scenes (5 indoor, 3 outdoor). While providing ~10,000 camera viewpoints, the semantic and structural diversity remains limited.

The 3D scene construction and novel-view exploration aspects (Sections 3.4 and 4.5) are evaluated purely qualitatively. There are no quantitative benchmarks against existing panorama-to-3D or scene generation methods (e.g., LayerPano3D, DreamCube, WonderWorld) regarding novel view synthesis quality or 3D mesh reconstruction accuracy.

Geometry prediction performance on distance estimation lags behind recent monocular estimators such as MoGe (Table 3), which may contribute to the bumpy reconstructed surfaces mentioned in the limitations.

strengths: Comprehensive and Versatile Unified Formulation: OmniX successfully establishes a unified paradigm redirecting pre-trained 2D flow matching models (FLUX.1-dev) to panoramic generation, dense intrinsic perception (albedo, roughness, metallic), geometry estimation (distance, surface normal), and inpainting-based completion.

Valuable New Benchmark (PanoX): The introduction of PanoX addresses an important gap in omnidirectional visual understanding. Providing dense pixel-aligned ground truth for geometry and PBR materials across both indoor and outdoor environments provides a valuable asset for future research in panoramic inverse rendering.

Insightful Architectural Exploration and Ablations: The systematic comparison between Shared-Branch, Shared-Adapter, and Separate-Adapter provides clear empirical validation for the proposed design. The ablation studies regarding camera rays and joint vs. independent modeling of geometry/material channels offer useful findings for the community.

Strong Quantitative Perception Results: OmniX outperforms existing inverse rendering and intrinsic decomposition baselines by significant margins on unseen scenes (PanoX-OutDomain), while also achieving competitive performance against specialized monocular geometry estimators.

Downstream Graphics Integration: The paper demonstrates practical downstream utility by translating predicted panoramic representations into textured meshes compatible with standard graphics workflows (Blender), including PBR relighting and rigid-body physical simulations.
weaknesses: Fragmented Multi-Model Pipeline: Rather than a single multi-task model capable of joint multi-modal inference, OmniX requires training and deploying 12 separate LoRA adapter models (one for each modality and task variant). This introduces considerable training overhead and makes inference cumbersome.

Lack of Quantitative Evaluation for 3D Scenes and Completion: While 2D perception metrics (PSNR, LPIPS, depth/normal errors) are thoroughly reported, the resulting 3D reconstructions, multi-step interactive completions, and novel view syntheses are only showcased qualitatively without quantitative benchmarks or user studies.

Mesh Reconstruction Artifacts and Generalization in the Wild: Reconstructing 3D meshes purely via spherical unprojection of distance maps frequently suffers from stretching, boundary tearing, and surface bumps, as acknowledged in the limitations. Furthermore, estimating specular/metallic properties in-the-wild remains challenging due to the synthetic-to-real gap and lack of physical illumination constraints in 2D priors.

strengths: Comprehensive exploration of adapter designs: The comparison between Shared-Branch, Shared-Adapter, and Separate-Adapter provides clear insights into effectively adapting large flow matching DiT backbones (FLUX.1-dev) for multi-condition and perception tasks.

Introduction of PanoX dataset: Dense panoramic annotations covering both indoor and outdoor environments with complete PBR channels (albedo, roughness, metallic, normal, distance) address a noticeable void in public panoramic benchmark datasets.

Strong 2D intrinsic decomposition performance: OmniX shows convincing quantitative and qualitative improvements over baselines such as DiffusionRenderer, IDArb, and MGNet on unseen out-of-domain panoramas for material parameter extraction.
Demonstration of downstream graphics compatibility: The pipeline shows end-to-end feasibility of taking single images/panoramas into Blender for relighting and dynamic physical simulation.
weaknesses: Overstated model unification: Although pitched as a unified framework, the system relies on training 12 distinct adapter/LoRA models for the individual tasks (depth, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic, completion variants). This represents a collection of task-specific models rather than a genuinely unified or joint multi-task representation.

Lack of quantitative 3D scene evaluation: The core claim revolves around generating 'graphics-ready 3D scenes', yet the evaluation in Section 4 is almost entirely restricted to 2D image-space metrics (PSNR, LPIPS, depth/normal error). There is no quantitative benchmarking for 3D reconstruction quality (e.g., Chamfer distance, F-score against ground truth 3D scene geometry) or novel view synthesis / relighting fidelity.

Naive 3D reconstruction and mesh artifacts: Directly back-projecting the predicted panoramic distance map into vertices and connecting neighboring pixels via spherical UV unwrapping inherently produces topological artifacts, stretching at depth discontinuities, and bumpy surfaces, as acknowledged in the limitations.

Limited diversity in dataset creation: PanoX is constructed from only 8 distinct synthetic 3D assets/scenes (5 indoor, 3 outdoor). While 10,000 viewpoints are rendered, the underlying semantic and material diversity remains narrow.

Insufficient evaluation of interactive completion: The interactive multi-step scene exploration relies on occlusion-aware masks and inpainting, but the paper does not systematically quantify multi-step consistency, cumulative geometric drift, or texture seams over extended trajectories.

strengths: A versatile and comprehensive framework (OmniX) that bridges panoramic 2D generative priors (Flow Matching / Flux) with intrinsic scene decomposition and 3D graphics-ready scene reconstruction.

The proposed circular synchronization technique is an elegant, training-free architectural modification that enforces circular translation equivariance across both convolutions and RoPE-based attention layers, effectively resolving equirectangular seam artifacts without heuristic blending.

The introduction of PanoX provides a valuable synthetic omnidirectional benchmark containing pixel-aligned multimodal annotations (distance, normals, albedo, roughness, metallic) for both indoor and outdoor environments.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across panoramic generation, intrinsic decomposition, and geometry estimation, supported by informative ablation studies examining adapter architectures and pre-trained prior transferability.
weaknesses: While framed as a 'unified framework', the practical system relies on 12 independently trained LoRA adapter models (for generation, each perceptual attribute, and masked completion variants) rather than a truly unified multi-task network. In fact, supplementary Table S4 shows that jointly modeling distance and normals degraded performance, highlighting limitations in multi-task synergy.

The PanoX dataset, while containing 10,000 camera viewpoints, is rendered from only eight synthetic 3D scenes (five indoor, three outdoor). This limited scene-level diversity introduces risks of stylistic overfitting, particularly for material properties like metallic and roughness.

Computational overhead is significant. Because the backbone is based on the 12B-parameter Flux.1-dev model, constructing a full PBR-ready scene requires sequential multi-step flow sampling passes across multiple adapters (RGB generation, depth, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic), yet the paper lacks discussion of runtime, memory footprint, or sampling latency.

The 3D scene reconstruction pipeline relies on naive spherical mesh unprojection from a single panoramic distance map followed by iterative inpainting. This mechanism is prone to geometric stretching, boundary distortion, and error accumulation during progressive camera movements.

strengths: A well-motivated and cohesive framework that bridges 2D flow-matching models with full panoramic perception (depth, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic) to produce graphics-ready assets with PBR material properties.

Circular Synchronization is a clean, training-free architectural modification that enforces circular translation equivariance across both convolutions and RoPE-based DiT attention layers, effectively solving seam artifacts without degrading generation quality.

The introduction of PanoX, a high-quality multimodal panoramic dataset covering both indoor and outdoor scenes with complete dense geometric and PBR material annotations, providing a useful resource for the community.

Extensive experimental results across multiple tasks (image-to-panorama generation, intrinsic decomposition, and geometry estimation) demonstrating significant quantitative and qualitative gains over competing methods.
weaknesses: The 3D scene generation and reconstruction application (Section 3.4 and 4.5), while central to the title and motivation, is evaluated mostly qualitatively in Blender without quantitative 3D mesh reconstruction metrics (such as Chamfer Distance or novel-view synthesis PSNR/LPIPS against ground-truth 3D scenes).

Dataset diversity is somewhat constrained: PanoX is constructed from only 8 distinct synthetic environments (5 indoor, 3 outdoor), which may limit broad geometric and aesthetic diversity in learned priors.

System complexity and computational overhead: maintaining and deploying up to 12 separate LoRA/adapter configurations based on the large Flux.1-dev model involves substantial training and inference costs.

strengths: Comprehensive and unified formulation: The paper effectively addresses panorama generation, dense intrinsic/geometric perception (distance, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic), and inpainting-based scene completion within a single unified flow-matching framework.

Principled circular synchronization: The proposed training-free structural adaptation enforces circular translation equivariance across both circular convolutions in the VAE and RoPE-based attention in the DiT, effectively resolving seam discontinuities without modifying pre-trained model weights.

Valuable dataset contribution (PanoX): Constructing a multi-modal synthetic panoramic dataset covering both indoor and outdoor scenes with pixel-aligned PBR materials (albedo, roughness, metallic) and geometric annotations (distance, normals) fills an important gap in panoramic inverse rendering and generation benchmarks.

Strong empirical results: The method achieves competitive or state-of-the-art results across perspective-to-panorama generation, intrinsic property decomposition, and surface normal estimation compared to specialized baselines.

Extensive ablation studies: The paper systematically evaluates adapter architectures, the influence of 2D generative pre-trained priors, camera ray conditioning, and joint versus independent modality modeling.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative 3D scene evaluation: While the paper positions graphics-ready 3D scene construction as a central application (showing qualitative Blender renderings of novel views, relighting, and simulation), it lacks quantitative benchmark evaluation for 3D reconstruction fidelity (e.g., Chamfer distance, surface error) or novel view synthesis quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS).

Model proliferation and inference complexity: OmniX trains 12 distinct adapter/LoRA configurations across the different tasks and modalities. Because independent predictions generally outperform joint predictions across modalities, generating a full PBR-ready scene requires multiple successive diffusion sampling passes, leading to heavy computational and latency overhead.

Limited scene diversity in PanoX: Although PanoX contains 10,000 viewpoints, they are rendered from only eight synthetic base environments (five indoor, three outdoor), which may limit the structural and semantic diversity needed for out-of-domain in-the-wild generalization.

Geometric precision limitations: As acknowledged by the authors, distance prediction can produce uneven surfaces that lead to bumpy reconstructed meshes, and metric depth accuracy remains behind established specialized monocular geometry estimators like MoGe.
